questions.prompt: A build prints its real errors to stderr. `npm test | grep FAIL` finds nothing, but the errors are clearly visible when you scroll. Why?
options: npm writes errors to stderr, and a pipe carries only stdout — you need `2>&1`
The pipe was too fast and grep missed the lines
questions.explanation: Two separate streams leave every program. `|` wires stdout only, so stderr went straight to your screen and never reached grep. `npm test 2>&1 | grep FAIL` folds stderr into stdout first. Option D is a real gotcha (`grep -i` fixes it) but it isn't why you saw nothing.

questions.prompt: You need to run a 10-minute migration, and you must close your terminal for a meeting and reconnect afterwards without killing it. Which is right?
options: `migration.sh > log.txt &` — the ampersand detaches it from the shell
`migration.sh > log.txt` — redirecting output already detaches it
`tmux new -s migrate`, run it inside, then detach with Ctrl-b d and reattach later
Leave the terminal open and lock the screen
questions.explanation: A backgrounded job is still a child of your shell; closing the shell sends it a hangup. Only tmux (or nohup/disown combined with the right conditions) survives a closed window. The ampersand and `>` solve *your attention*, not the terminal's lifetime.

questions.prompt: Why does `echo hi | cd src` leave you in the same directory, but `(cd src && pwd)` prints the src path?
options: `cd` is not a real command and only works inside parentheses
The left side of a pipe runs in a subshell whose `cd` is discarded on exit; parentheses create one you can use deliberately
The pipe runs too fast for `cd` to take effect
Pipes always reset the working directory before running
questions.explanation: `cd` changes the shell's own state, and a piped command runs in a child subshell — its directory change dies with it. Parentheses are how you ask for exactly that behaviour when you want it: the cd applies inside, and vanishes after. Option C is wrong; it is not timing.
